case_title: Ranjeet Singh @ Dara v. State of Madhya Pradesh
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (step-son of the victim); the appellant was a regular visitor to the house
evidence_type: Circumstantial evidence; oral evidence of witnesses; medical evidence (post-mortem report); documentary evidence; recovery of the sword and blood-stained items
confession: Oral statement made when the door was opened that the accused had killed the victim; recounted in the evidence and treated by the Court as part of the oral evidence connecting the accused, not separately analysed as a confession
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 5000, in default one year rigorous imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 469 of 2000) dismissed; conviction under s.302 IPC confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim, a woman, lived on the first floor of a family house with her adult son; a relative of the accused lived on the ground floor with his wife. The accused, who lived in another city, was a regular visitor to the house. On the day of the incident the accused arrived by car at about 11.30 a.m. The ground-floor occupant's wife offered the accused a meal, and the accused said the accused would eat with the ground-floor occupant. Shortly afterwards the household maid heard screams from the victim's room. At about 2.30 p.m. the victim's son came to collect money and found the room locked from inside. He heard the accused talking on a telephone and asked the accused to open the door, which the accused refused. The ground-floor occupant also asked for the door to be opened, and the accused replied that the door would be opened only when police arrived. When police arrived, the accused opened the door and stated that the accused had killed the victim. The accused was holding a blood-stained sword, and the accused's clothing and hands were blood-stained. The victim was lying on a bed, her body smeared with blood. The sword, its sheath, blood-stained bedsheets and a gold bala were seized, and the accused's clothing and hand washings were taken. The post-mortem examination recorded seventeen injuries, all but three of them incised wounds that could be caused by a sharp-edged weapon such as a sword. The accused gave no explanation for being in the locked room or for holding the blood-stained sword. An injury report on the accused recorded an examination time of 11.30 a.m., which the accused relied on to suggest being in police custody at that time; its author was not examined as a witness.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; seventeen injuries, mostly incised wounds from a sharp-edged weapon such as a sword, to the abdomen, head, limbs and buttock
motive: alleged: apprehension that the father would favour the illegitimate son (PW-11) over the legitimate sons; the Court did not decide the motive
key_evidence_accepted: Oral evidence of PW-1, PW-9, PW-11, PW-12 and PW-13 (the accused's presence in the locked room, the statement at the door, the blood-stained sword); post-mortem report Ex. P-11; seizure of the sword and blood-stained items; the failure to explain presence and the sword
witness_credibility: PW-11 was cross-examined at length without anything useful elicited and his account was consistent with PW-13; PW-10's naming of another family member was held to be possibly confusion, and the discrepancies noticed by the courts below did not justify discarding the prosecution evidence
post_offence_conduct: Refused to open the locked door to the son and the ground-floor occupant and said he would open it only when police arrived; then opened the door and stated he had killed the victim
trial_duration: offence: 6.9.1997; trial judgment: 7.3.2000; High Court: 13.3.2006; Supreme Court: 20.9.2010
legal_representation: Appellant: K.T.S. Tulsi, Senior Advocate (with Ram Nivas, Raj Kamal, A.P. Dhamija, Sanjeev Malhotra); State: C.D. Singh (with Sunny Choudhary, Shashank Parihar, Sakshi Kakkar)
investigation_status: FIR registered as Case No. 165/97 under s.302 IPC; accused arrested; charge sheet and trial completed (conviction at trial)
procedural_irregularity: Defence argued FIR registration was delayed and a copy was not sent to the Magistrate for five days; the courts below found no prejudice and sufficient explanation, and the Court did not find a fatal irregularity
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302 IPC, life imprisonment and fine Rs. 5000; High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction confirmed; Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Delay in sending FIR copy caused no prejudice and the delay was explained by PW-13; the delay alone cannot discard the prosecution evidence; the appellant had a motive; the appellant was caught red-handed with blood-stained hands and sword; Ex. D5 is falsified by Ex. P22
defence_argument: False implication; the real culprit was shielded; the FIR was deliberately delayed; investigation incomplete; the appellant was in police custody at 11.45 hrs for medical examination; injuries to his hands made wielding a sword impossible; discrepancies in the evidence of PW-10, PW-11 and PW-13
legal_principle_applied: In a case based primarily on circumstantial evidence, the chain must be complete and consistent only with guilt (Hanumant); under Article 136 the Court interferes with concurrent findings of fact only in very exceptional circumstances; no such circumstances were shown
precedent_relied_upon: Hanumant Govind Nargundkar v. State of M.P. 1952 SCR 1091 (relied on); Ganga Kumar Srivastava v. State of Bihar (2005) 6 SCC 211 (principles on Article 136 interference; held not to apply to the appellant's case); also referred to: Rangaiah (2008) 16 SCC 737; Ghurey Lal (2008) 10 SCC 450; Abdulwahab Abdulmajid Baloch (2009) 11 SCC 625; Budh Singh (2006) 9 SCC 731; Rajeevan (2003) 3 SCC 355; Dharamver (2010) 4 SCC 469; Rabindra Mahto (2006) 10 SCC 432; Aqeel Ahmed (2008) 16 SCC 372
